passages.happening:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘Take vengeance on the Midianites for the Israelites. After that, you will be gathered to your people’” (verses 1-2).

Moses sends a thousand men from each tribe, twelve thousand in all. Phinehas the priest goes with them, carrying the holy vessels and the trumpets (verses 3-6).

“Then they waged war against Midian, as the LORD had commanded Moses, and they killed every male” (verse 7). Among the dead are the five kings of Midian. “They also killed Balaam son of Beor with the sword” (verse 8).

The Israelites take the women and children captive, carry off the herds and goods, burn the towns and camps, and bring everything to Moses and Eleazar at the camp on the plains of Moab (verses 9-12).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the hardest chapters in the Bible. A reader should know that before starting, and should not be surprised to find it painful. These notes will say what the chapter says, as plainly as they can. They will not soften it, and they will not defend what cannot be defended.

The chapter finishes the story of chapter 25. At Peor, Israelite men were drawn into the worship of Baal, and a plague killed twenty-four thousand. God then told Moses to treat the Midianites involved as enemies (25:16-18). Now that command is carried out. It is the last act of Moses' life as leader.

The war is called ‘the LORD’s vengeance’ (verse 3). In the Old Testament vengeance belongs to God. The word means the just repayment of a wrong. It does not mean private revenge. The same conviction lies behind God's later words, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32:35).

Who the Midianites were matters. They were a loose group of desert peoples who ranged widely, and Genesis traces them to a son of Abraham (Genesis 25:2). Moses had lived among Midianites for many years. His wife Zipporah was one, and her father Jethro had helped and advised him. So this was not a war on a people as a people. The group in view seems to be the Midianites settled near Moab and joined with it against Israel. Their five leaders appear again in Joshua as chiefs allied with King Sihon (Joshua 13:21). One of them, Zur, was the father of Cozbi, the woman of chapter 25.

Nor did the war end Midian. In the time of the judges, Midianites were strong enough to oppress Israel for seven years (Judges 6:1-2). Whatever verse 7 means by ‘every male’, it describes a limited action against one group.

Balaam dies here, among the kings. The man who said, ‘Let me die the death of the righteous’ (23:10), is killed with those he advised. Verse 16 will say why.

War in Israel was hedged with ritual. A priest went with the army. Those who had killed were unclean afterward and had to stay outside the camp. Even in a war God commanded, death defiled.
passages.later:
Joshua names the same five chiefs: Moses killed ‘the chiefs of Midian (Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba), the princes of Sihon who lived in the land’ (Joshua 13:21).

Paul quotes God's words about vengeance in order to forbid Christians to take any: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19). He goes on, “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).
passages.asks: Scripture says that vengeance belongs to God, and the New Testament draws from that the conclusion that it does not belong to his people. Ask what wrong done to you, or to people you love, you are waiting to repay. And ask what it would mean to leave it with God.

passages.happening:
Moses, Eleazar and the leaders go out to meet the returning army. “But Moses was angry with the officers of the army” (verse 14). “Have you spared all the women?” he asks (verse 15).

He gives his reason. ‘Look, these women caused the sons of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to turn unfaithfully against the LORD at Peor, so that the plague struck the congregation of the LORD’ (verse 16).

Then he gives the order. “So now, kill all the boys, as well as every woman who has had relations with a man, but spare for yourselves every girl who has never had relations with a man” (verses 17-18).
passages.hearers:
These verses must be read as they stand. Moses orders that the captive boys be killed, and every woman who has slept with a man. He orders that the girls be kept alive for the Israelites. The boys were children. Verse 35 gives the number of girls kept as 32,000.

There is no way to make this easy to read, and no one should try. A reader who is sickened by it is reading it rightly.

Several things can be said about what the text does and does not say. None of them removes the difficulty.

Verse 16 gives the reason Moses states. The plot at Peor is here revealed to have come from Balaam's advice. It worked through these women, and it cost Israel twenty-four thousand lives. In Moses' eyes the army had brought into the camp the very means by which Israel had nearly been destroyed.

The reason covers the women. It does not cover the boys. They had done nothing, and the text gives no reason for their deaths. Israel's own law says, “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16).

The order in verses 17 and 18 is given in the text as Moses' own words. God's command in verse 2 was to take vengeance on Midian. The chapter does not record God telling Moses what to do with the captives. Some readers lay weight on that. But it must also be said that the chapter records no rebuke of Moses, and that in verse 25 God gives instructions for dividing the captives. The text does not offer an easy way out here, and these notes do not invent one.

As for the girls, the text says they were to be kept ‘for yourselves’. It does not say what became of them. They were girls and young women whose fathers, mothers and brothers had been killed, and they were taken into the households of the people who had done it. Their own voices are not in the story. Israel's law of war did set limits on the treatment of a captive woman. A man who wished to marry one had to give her a month to mourn her parents, could not sell her, and if he later turned from her had to let her go free (Deuteronomy 21:10-14). Those limits were real in their world. They do not make the taking of these girls right, and these notes do not say that it was.
passages.later:
The prophet Ezekiel states the principle that makes this passage so hard: “The soul who sins is the one who will die. A son will not bear the iniquity of his father” (Ezekiel 18:20).

When two disciples wanted to call down fire on a village that had refused Jesus, “Jesus turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55). And he taught, “But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).
passages.hard:
How can this be in the Bible? How have Christians understood it?

Christians who receive this book as God's word have answered in several ways. Each answer has a cost, and no honest reader claims that any of them makes the chapter painless.

Some stress the setting. This was a judgment on a particular group for a deliberate plot to destroy Israel, after a plague had killed thousands. God, the judge of all, has the right to judge, and he sometimes judged through human armies, as he later judged Israel itself through Assyria and Babylon. The cost of this answer is the children. It has nothing to say for the boys that does not leave the grief where it was.

Some stress the limits. This was one act at one time. It was never made a pattern for later wars. Israel's law of war elsewhere restrains violence, and Midian was not wiped out.

Some read such chapters as recording the customs and the language of ancient war honestly, without holding them up as right, and say that the teaching of Christ must govern how Christians read them. Others reply that this reading can weaken the authority of Scripture.

Many believers hold these together. They confess that God is just, and they admit that the text remains painful. These notes take no side among the readings. Abraham once asked God, “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25), and the Bible does not rebuke him for asking.

One thing is not in doubt. No one may use this chapter to justify violence against any person or people. It is no warrant for killing prisoners, for harming children, or for taking women or girls. It names a people of the ancient world and says nothing about any nation or conflict today. Rape, forced marriage and the abuse of captives are grave evils, and this chapter gives no one leave to commit them.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The site's pages on the violence of the Old Testament and on the command to destroy the Canaanites go further.
passages.asks: This passage should trouble a reader. Ask what you do with a page of the Bible that sickens you: turn it quickly, explain it away, or bring it to God as Abraham did. And ask whose suffering in war today you have learned not to see, and what the command of Jesus to love enemies asks of you about it.

passages.happening:
Moses tells the soldiers, “All of you who have killed a person or touched the dead are to remain outside the camp for seven days. On the third day and the seventh day you are to purify both yourselves and your captives” (verse 19). Clothing, leather, goat's hair and wood are to be purified too (verse 20).

Eleazar adds the rule for metals. Gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin and lead, ‘everything that can withstand the fire’, must be put through fire and then purified with the water of purification. Everything else must pass through water (verses 22-23). On the seventh day the soldiers wash their clothes, and then they may come into the camp (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
This short passage says something easy to miss. The soldiers have fought in a war that God commanded, and they come back unclean. They may not walk into the camp. They must wait outside for a week and be sprinkled on the third day and the seventh with the water of chapter 19, the water made with the ashes of the red heifer.

In Israel's law, contact with death always defiled, whatever the cause. A man who had killed in battle was in the same state as a man who had buried his father. He was not fit to come near the place where the living God lived until he had been cleansed.

So the law refuses to treat killing as a clean thing, even when it was commanded. There is no victory parade into the camp. There is a week of waiting outside it. The captives are purified too.

The uncleanness in this passage is ritual, as chapter 19 explained. But the picture is a truthful one. Killing marks those who do it. A people that has shed blood cannot simply go on as before.
passages.later:
King David was not allowed to build the temple, for a reason like this one. God said to him, “You are not to build a house for My Name, because you are a man of war who has spilled blood” (1 Chronicles 28:3).

Isaiah saw a day when the tools of war would not be needed: “They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor train anymore for war” (Isaiah 2:4).
passages.asks: Men who had fought at God's command still had to stop outside the camp and be cleansed. Ask what you have done, even rightly or under orders, that has left a mark on you and has never been brought to God. And ask how your community receives people who come home from war: whether it gives them time and a way back.

passages.happening:
God tells Moses to count everything captured, ‘both of man and beast’, and to divide it in two: half for the soldiers who fought, half for the rest of the people (verses 26-27).

From the soldiers' half, one in every five hundred goes to Eleazar the priest ‘as an offering to the LORD’. From the people's half, one in every fifty goes to the Levites (verses 28-30).

The totals are given: 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, ‘and 32,000 women who had not slept with a man’ (verses 32-35). Each half is listed, and the shares for the priest and the Levites are handed over, ‘as the LORD had commanded Moses’ (verses 41, 47).
passages.hearers:
After the violence comes bookkeeping. Numbers likes lists and totals, and this is one of its most careful.

The rule of division became a custom in Israel. Those who fought and those who stayed behind shared alike. David later made the same ruling for his own men (1 Samuel 30:24-25). And from each half a portion went to God, through the priest and the Levites. The Hebrew word for this portion, mekhes, a levy, is used only in this chapter. It was a way of saying that the victory and its goods were not simply the army's.

The figures are very large. They raise the same questions as the census totals, and the note on 1:20-46 sets out how those are read.

A reader cannot pass over what is being counted. The lists set human beings beside sheep, cattle and donkeys. Thirty-two thousand girls are divided as shares. Thirty-two of them go to the priest as the LORD's tribute, and three hundred and twenty to the Levites. The text reports this in the same even voice as the rest.

That is how captives were treated across the ancient world, and Israel here does as its world did. It should be named for what it was. These were people, made in the image of God, and they were handed out as property. The hard question below says more.
passages.later:
Job, speaking of his own servants, saw what such lists hide: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (Job 31:15).

The New Testament names those who trade in human beings among the lawless. Paul's list of people the law condemns includes ‘slave traders’ (1 Timothy 1:10).
passages.hard:
The girls are counted as plunder and shared out, some to the sanctuary. How should a reader think about that?

That is in the text, and it cannot be explained away. These notes do not defend it.

What became of the thirty-two given to the priest is not said. The law of Moses counts the sacrifice of children among the things the LORD hates (Deuteronomy 12:31), so that is not what is meant. They were handed to Eleazar as the animals were (verse 29). They were still captives, with their own families dead.

The Bible's own teaching presses against what this chapter records. Every person is made in God's image (Genesis 1:27). The law punished kidnapping with death (Exodus 21:16). It commanded Israel to love the foreigner (Leviticus 19:34). Christians read these verses in the ways set out in the note on verses 13 to 18, and no reading makes the taking of these girls good.

No one may use this passage to excuse the owning, buying, selling or forcing of any person.

A word for anyone who has been sold, traded, or forced to work or to do sexual acts by someone who controls them, or who is in that place now. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The chapter counts people in the same list as animals. Ask where people are counted that way now: in what trades, in what places, in what you buy. And ask whose names and stories are missing from the accounts you rely on.

passages.t: Not one missing, and an offering of gold
passages.happening:
The officers come to Moses and say, “Your servants have counted the soldiers under our command, and not one of us is missing” (verse 49).

They bring the gold they took, ‘armlets, bracelets, rings, earrings, and necklaces’, as an offering ‘to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD’ (verse 50). It weighs 16,750 shekels (verse 52).

Moses and Eleazar bring the gold into the tent ‘as a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD’ (verse 54).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with a report and a gift.

The report is that not one of the twelve thousand was lost. The officers take that as God's protection.

Their response is worth noticing. No one ordered this offering. The officers bring it themselves, and they give their reason: ‘to make atonement for ourselves’. Men who have come home safe from a victory feel the need of atonement. The text does not say exactly why. The law had said that whenever Israel's men were counted, each was to pay a ransom for his life (Exodus 30:12), and the officers have just counted their men. They may also simply have known that they had come through bloodshed and stood in need of mercy.

Either way the chapter does not end in triumph. It ends with soldiers giving up their plunder and asking to be put right with God. The gold is placed in the tent as a memorial, a reminder kept before God and the people.

With this chapter Moses' work as a leader in war is finished. God had said that after it he would be gathered to his people.
passages.later:
The law of the census may lie behind the officers' words: “each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life when he is counted” (Exodus 30:12).

The New Testament turns the church's warfare away from people altogether: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness” (Ephesians 6:12). And it says that the judgment of God on sin fell at last on Christ himself, who ‘bore our sins in His body on the tree’ (1 Peter 2:24).
passages.asks: The officers came home whole and felt the need of atonement. Ask whether your successes ever send you to God in the same way your failures do. And ask what you have gained at someone else's cost, and what it would mean to lay it down.
